w: What's tested How insulin works and how diabetes is diagnosed Which insulin to use for a meal and which for all day Each diabetes drug: how it works, its main side effects, who shouldn't take it Which drugs cause low blood sugar or weight gain, and which to pick for which patient Low blood sugar in the dental chair The big picture Diabetes means high blood sugar because the body makes too little insulin, or the body doesn't respond to it, or usually both. Type 1: the immune system destroyed the insulin-making beta cells, so the patient needs insulin. Type 2: the body resists insulin and doesn't make enough. Prediabetes is the zone just below diabetes, and it can be reversed with weight loss and lifestyle change. Secondary diabetes has another cause, like steroids or Cushing syndrome: treat the cause. Dentists see it first sometimes: bad gum disease, slow healing, mouth infections, dry mouth, and low blood sugar during appointments. Insulin basics Beta cells make proinsulin, which splits into insulin plus C-peptide in equal amounts. Injected insulin has no C-peptide. No C-peptide = the pancreas makes no insulin. GLUT4 is the transporter insulin moves to the surface of muscle and fat cells. Other GLUTs, like GLUT1 for the brain, don't need insulin. Insulin also pushes potassium into cells. That's why insulin plus glucose treats a high potassium. Complications Small vessels: nerves, kidneys, eyes (neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy). Big vessels: heart attacks, leg artery disease, stroke. The hyperosmolar state kills more often than DKA. Diagnosis: you need two A1C 6.5 percent or higher (prediabetes 5.7 to 6.4). Fasting glucose 126 or higher (prediabetes 100 to 125). A 2-hour glucose tolerance test of 200 or higher, or a random glucose above 200. A1C shows about 3 months of sugar, because sugar sticks to hemoglobin for good and red cells live about that long. Insulins: fast for meals, slow for all day Rapid: lispro, aspart, glulisine. Start in 5 to 15 minutes, last about 4 hours. Taken right before a meal. Inhaled Afrezza: works in a minute or two. Regular: peaks at about 3 hours, gone by about 8. NPH: starts in 2 to 4 hours, too slow for a meal. Protamine slows it down. Long: glargine, detemir. Flat, all day. Ultra-long: degludec, over 42 hours. Basal-bolus: one long insulin a day for the background, plus a rapid one before each meal. Skip the meal, skip the rapid dose. Regular and NPH are sold without a prescription. Insulin side effects: low blood sugar, weight gain, injection-site fat changes, and a short-term worsening of retinopathy. The two questions for every pill or shot Does it cause low blood sugar? Does it cause weight gain? Anything that squeezes out insulin does both: insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides. TZDs cause weight gain but not lows. GLP-1 drugs cause weight loss. Metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors are neutral. The drugs, one line each Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride): close the beta cell's potassium channel, so insulin comes out. Need working beta cells. Wear off over time. Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction); careful with G6PD deficiency, liver and kidney disease (mostly glyburide). Meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide): the same, but quick, taken with meals. Not after a sulfonylurea fails. Metformin: first-line. Liver makes less sugar. Doesn't lower a normal sugar, so no lows. Side effects: stomach upset, low B12, lactic acidosis. Stop if eGFR is under 30. TZDs (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone): turn on PPAR-gamma in fat. Swelling, heart failure, weight gain, macular edema. Not in class III or IV heart failure. GLP-1 drugs (exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide): more insulin only when sugar is high, less glucagon, slower stomach. Weight loss. Nausea. Slow other pills like antibiotics and the birth-control pill. Boxed warning: thyroid C-cell tumors. Semaglutide also comes as a daily tablet. DPP-4 inhibitors (the -gliptins): keep your own GLP-1 around longer. Pills, once a day. No lows, weight neutral, weak. Avoid in heart failure except sitagliptin. Linagliptin: no kidney dose change. Acarbose, miglitol: block carb digestion in the gut. Gas, bloating, diarrhea. Pramlintide: fake amylin, injected before meals; lows when used with insulin. SGLT2 inhibitors (the -gliflozins): you pee out the sugar. Yeast infections, UTIs, peeing a lot, low blood pressure and dizziness. Help heart failure (dapagliflozin is approved for it). Canagliflozin and ertugliflozin: boxed warning for amputation. Colesevelam: binds other drugs in the gut (warfarin, glyburide, thyroxine). Name tricks -gliflozin sounds like flushing the sugar away: SGLT2 inhibitors. -gliptin: DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, alogliptin). -glitazone: TZDs (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone). -glinide: meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide). -glutide and -natide: GLP-1 drugs (liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, exenatide, lixisenatide). Sulfonylureas you see in charts: glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride. Why the side effects make sense Drugs that squeeze out insulin act whatever the sugar is, so they can push it too low. Metformin doesn't touch a normal sugar, so it rarely causes lows. GLP-1 drugs slow the stomach. That is why people feel full and lose weight, why they feel sick at first, and why other pills get absorbed more slowly. SGLT2 inhibitors put sugar in the urine. Sugar feeds germs (yeast infections, UTIs) and pulls water out (lots of urine, low blood pressure, dizziness). TZDs hold on to fluid. Extra fluid means swelling, heart failure and macular edema. Acarbose leaves carbs undigested in the gut, where they cause gas, bloating and diarrhea. Insulin builds tissue (it is anabolic), so it adds weight. Picking a drug Healthy, new type 2: metformin. Overweight: GLP-1 drug, unless there's a history of thyroid cancer. Heart failure: SGLT2 inhibitor; never a TZD. Bad kidneys: no metformin under eGFR 30. Low sugar in the chair Typical story: took a rapid insulin, skipped breakfast. Sweaty, shaky, confused. If awake: juice, regular soda or glucose tablets. If unresponsive: glucagon, injected or as a nasal spray.
